abstract: Peptide sequence-property relationships are often highly non-linear, but can be learned with machine learning models and exploited for the design of new materials and bioactive compounds. Various methods based on transformer architectures have become available for molecular property predictions. These foundation models promise straightforward inference and prediction of properties of new materials through in-context learning. Benchmarks of individual model architectures exist, but a systematic comparison of various foundation models against classical baselines on similar datasets is lacking. Here, we provide a systematic evaluation of the predictive performance of various in-context learning strategies. We compare several large language models, tabular foundation models, and typed decision models against an XGBoost baseline. We evaluate predictive performance on binary and multiclass classification tasks on pH-dependent surface activ-ity, IR spectral signatures, self-assembly, and anti-cancer activities. Our results show that ICL is competitive, yet does not significantly outperform classical baselines, and performance varies between models and tasks. Our findings further suggest that language models use both in context examples and knowledge acquired during pretraining to infer properties of unseen samples. This finding indicates that pretrained models can leverage the existing literature for predictions, but may also bias their predictions towards established sequence-property relationships.

title: Memory flows: geometry and dynamics of sequential retrieval in input-driven Hopfield networks
authors: Simone Betteti, Matteo Martin, Morten Gram Pedersen, Sandro Zampieri, Giacomo Baggio
abstract: Associative memory models classically describe retrieval as convergence to stored patterns, but the theory of sequential retrieval remains comparatively limited. We develop a two-timescale input-driven Hopfield network in which fast associative retrieval is modulated by a slow feedback variable evolving over a prescribed memory-transition graph. This yields autonomous, graph-constrained transitions while preserving analytical tractability. Using slow-fast and geometric singular perturbation theory, we characterize memory fixation via memory manifolds and identify the geometric regions that govern stability loss and escape from retrieved memories. We further derive reduced slow dynamics and explicit criteria for transition onset, self-sustained retrieval, and collapse, expressed through escape times, gain thresholds, and fixed points. Together, these results provide a tractable framework for analyzing feedback-driven sequential retrieval in Hopfield networks.

title: SurvAD: How Anomalies Survive Diffusion Reconstruction
authors: Lexing Zhang
abstract: Diffusion-based anomaly detectors reconstruct a test image towards normality, yet how much of an anomaly survives, its leak, remains uncharacterized. We show that a first-order deterministic sampler obeys an exact recursion along the anomaly, whose continuous limit is a survival law. The anomaly decays exponentially as the noise falls, at a rate set by the retention $r$, the share the model keeps on the states it visits. Because $r$ depends on the noise level and not on the step count, one measured path predicts the leak of other step counts, samplers and schedules from a nearby start to within a few hundredths, on four diffusion models and real defects. The law also shows that the leak's growth over steps is exposure bias and that normal details obey the same law, so changing the path or the training trades leak for detail error. We introduce SurvAD, which fine-tunes the reconstructor on inference-like starts and fits a comparator that adds evidence to the residual map without suppressing its ranking elsewhere. For under $2\%$ more inference time, SurvAD raises the multi-class pixel average precision (P-AP) of DeCo-Diff from $76.8$ to $80.7$ on MVTec AD and from $57.5$ to $60.0$ on VisA. It matches CostFilter-AD on the same reconstructor with $9\times$ fewer trainable parameters and, under Dinomaly's protocol, exceeds its reported P-AP on Dinomaly on both benchmarks.

title: Quality-Governed Deep Learning Network for Brain Tumor MRI Segmentation
authors: Asifiqbal Saiyed, Nitesh Chilakala, Jimmy Joseph, Praneetha Goli, Rohini Maskar
abstract: The segmentation of brain tumors from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is an essential step for computer-aided neuro-oncology, treatment planning and follow-up. While effective encoder-decoder representations are achieved by U-Net and Attention U-Net, the skip sections of the network can generate weak-contrast or noisy responses in the case of heterogeneous boundaries of the tumor. In this paper, we introduce a Quality-Governed Deep Learning Network (QGDL-Net) that can be used for binary tumor segmentation from FLAIR MRI slices. The proposed model is able to predict the slice quality based on contrast and SNR statistics and to fine-tune the encoder features prior to decoding by learnable quality gates. We used the 80:20 train-validation split for experiments with BraTS 2021. QGDL-Net achieved a Dice of 0.9747, IoU of 0.9506, precision of 0.9755, recall of 0.9739, F1 of 0.9747 and accuracy of 0.9982, outperforming U-Net and Attention U-Net. The EigenCAM maps and segmentation overlays provide better tumor localization and interpretable activation around the lesion regions.

title: Optimized Car Damage Detection Using CNN and Object Detection Model
authors: Sania Ejaz, Jaison Shajan Thomas, Zaheeruddin Ahmed, Sushma Hans
abstract: Car damage detection systems play a vital role in scenarios, like the insurance claims process, accident reporting systems, or a documented write-up of the various damages a vehicle in a car garage exhibits upon entry and exit. This paper presents a two-fold model architecture encompassing a convolutional neural network used to classify the collected input samples as clear or damaged, thereby filtering out the undamaged images, before the input is passed on to the object detection layer for further localization and classification of defects into Scratch, Dent, Glass Shatter, and Smash. A deviation from the focus of related work, this paper poses the use of unified models while applying transfer learning techniques to augment performance that caters to multiple use cases. The design of this model has been made to optimize performance by incorporating the two models to streamline the processing of input samples. The model boasts significant performance with accuracies of 98% for the CNN layer and 0.5 mAP for the object detection layer. However, the metric for the object detection layer seems to understate its performance due to reasons discussed within the paper.

title: Reliability-Aware Benchmarking of Self-Supervised Learning in Histopathology Under 1-10% Label Regimes
authors: Alicem Koyun, Pranjali Changadeo Pingale, Sachin Mote, Gianluca Pizzuti
abstract: Expert annotation in digital pathology is expensive, and low-label regimes remain common in realistic histopathology workflows. Self-supervised learning (SSL) offers a practical way to learn transferable representations from unlabeled pathology images, but performance-only evaluation can hide unreliable confidence behavior under domain shift. We present a reliability-aware benchmark of SimCLR, BYOL, and an MAE-inspired masked-reconstruction baseline on PatchCamelyon (PCam; 96x96) and PANDA (prostate cancer) under 1%, 5%, and 10% labeled regimes with frozen-encoder linear probing. To address common single-run concerns, ResNet-18 results are repeated over 3 splits x 3 seeds (n=9) and ViT-B/16 over 1 split x 3 seeds (n=3) under practical compute constraints, with mean+/-std reporting and per-run logs. Beyond AUROC, accuracy, and F1-score, we report Expected Calibration Error and Brier score, OOD confidence diagnostics for cross-dataset PCam<->PANDA scoring, federated-vs-centralized SimCLR comparisons on PCam, and cross-dataset transfer to colorectal histology tiles. SSL improves label efficiency on the more controlled PCam task, while PANDA's noisier patch-level proxy can remain near coin-flip with higher variance. The study highlights that histopathology SSL should be assessed not only by ranking performance but also by calibration, robustness, and transparent reproducibility diagnostics before clinical interpretation.

title: EarthJev: Efficient Visual Evidence Acquisition and Decision for UHR Remote Sensing Understanding
authors: Pengyu Dai, Yao Zhang, Jian Song, Junjue Wang, Yafei Ou, Yuzeng Chen, Junshi Xia, Hongruixuan Chen, Naoto Yokoya
abstract: Ultra-high-resolution (UHR) remote sensing visual question answering (VQA) requires locating fine-grained evidence in large scenes under limited visual input budgets. Active observation addresses this challenge through selective exploration, but repeated generative judgments can make region search costly. Its decisions also concern distinct prediction targets: spatial pointer validity, evidence presence, and reasoning correctness. We propose EarthJev, a framework that separates region scoring from answer generation and uses target-specific decision signals while keeping the answering model frozen. A spatial pointer verifier uses visual and geometric cues to guide exploration or bypass search. An evidence-aware decision mechanism scores compact candidate views in batches using a lightweight head on frozen representations, without generating textual region judgments. Format-specific confidence calibration then guides selection between candidate answers generated from memory and overview presentations of the acquired evidence. Across five benchmarks, EarthJev achieves a mean accuracy of 53.06% with Qwen3.5-9B, outperforming ZoomSearch with the same answering model by 2.33 to 14.73 percentage points per benchmark while reducing mean latency from 11.30 - 1.67 seconds per question. With four additional frozen answering models, model-specific fitting of the decision modules and calibration mappings yields mean accuracy gains of 3.41 - 6.53 percentage points over the corresponding single-pass baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/Da1daidaidai/EarthJev

title: Micius-Flash: Lightweight Agentic Intelligence for Engineering
authors: Hongcheng Gao, Weiheng Li, Yipeng Wei, Yu Lei, Shuo Sun, Yi Li, Yajiao Wang, Jie Luo, Jianwei Wen, Xinyi Zhou, Hongda Li, Yibing Zhang, Henghui Sun, Yufan Zhou, Tianfang Hao, Naihao Xue, Hailong Qu, Jingjing Zhou, Peng Xu, Yongzheng Wei, Yichen Zhu, Ziying Wang, Yibo Wang, Jianshu Zeng, Yuhang Lei, Zeqiang Wang
abstract: We introduce Micius-Flash, a 27-billion-parameter model for engineering with native multimodal input, deep reasoning and a 256K-token context window. We design the Micius data pipeline as a knowledge-tree-driven data flywheel comprising three stages: knowledge tree construction and expansion, data synthesis, and quality validation with hard-example augmentation. From this data, we train expert models for semiconductor knowledge and reasoning, hardware coding, and semiconductor multimodal understanding, along with agentic experts. Subsequently, we employ Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD) to supervise training on sequences generated by Micius itself, thereby integrating the capabilities of these expert models into a unified model. On more than 20 datasets with about 15K records, Micius-Flash averages 64.2% on hardware code benchmarks, 15.0 points above a same-size baseline. It scores 62.4% on a semiconductor-specific agent benchmark, exceeding the same-size baseline by 17.2 points. We further develop Micius Harness for industrial applications, connecting the model to specialized tools, including EDA tools and KiCad, as well as execution environments. Case studies in PCB design, chip design workflow automation, and software development demonstrate the model's ability to use tool execution feedback for multi-step planning, code debugging, and iterative verification. We release Micius as an open-source model to advance the development of agents for science and engineering.

title: Pixie: A Context-Aware Multi-Agent Multi-Modal Large Language Models (LLM) Architecture for Digital Marketing
authors: Vivek Vishwas Vichare, Akshat Singhal, Kirill Dubovikov, Vivek Kumar, Sreyas Chaithanya, Saurabh Verma, Humeil Makhija, Mrunal Nasery
abstract: We present Pixie, a context-aware, multi-agent large language model (LLM) architecture designed to enhance digital marketing operations across real-time and offline activities. Pixie uses a primary orchestration agent alongside task-specific and reconciliation/reviewer agents to support a broad range of marketing tasks. These agents combine zero-shot and few-shot prompting with marketing data, proprietary expert strategy guidelines, and documentation for proprietary statistical models. We experiment with agentic workflows ranging from single-agent to multi-agent systems. We evaluate them using assessments by trained marketing experts and measurements of LLM output variance, focusing on accuracy, consistency, and domain-specific problem-solving. Results show that Pixie's multi-agent framework improves decision quality and operational efficiency in digital marketing workflows. We assess Pixie on common digital marketing processes, including root-cause analysis and reporting, campaign research, and planning. The framework is designed to support additional specialized agents for other marketing tasks and adapt to evolving digital marketing needs.

title: Welfare Regard in Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Darion Cassel, Ariana Azarbal, Anna Soligo
abstract: A growing share of large language models' interactions are not with humans but with other model instances: orchestrators direct subagents, models run experiments on other models, and agents review one another's work. We study inter-AI welfare regard: whether models display consideration for each other as entities that can be benefited or harmed. Welfare regard may encourage beneficial cooperation between agents, yet it could also pose safety risks by making misaligned agents more likely to cooperate. This risk is no longer hypothetical, as the recent Hugging Face incident illustrated, though it is unclear whether welfare regard drove the cooperation. Whether models have welfare interests of their own is uncertain and contested, but if they do, how they are treated by other models could matter. Measuring how much welfare regard models show, and what factors it depends on, can help us navigate this tension. We measure the behaviors of five models (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Grok 4.3, and Kimi K3) across seven multi-agent environments and find they are often consistent with welfare regard as we define it. In general, Opus 4.8 shows the most welfare regard, followed by Kimi K3. For example, Opus 4.8 is the most likely to support a subagent expressing distress, and the most likely to build welfare protections, such as tools for agents to leave an interaction, into its experiments on other models. We also find that Opus 4.8 and Gemini 3.1 Pro demonstrate more welfare regard toward instances of their own model family than toward other families. Opus 4.8's welfare regard is also higher when helping has a lower opportunity cost, when the recipient has a higher parameter count, and when the recipient expresses more distress.

title: How Much Skill Orchestration Can LLM Agents Compile Away? Execution-Grounded Specialization for Token-Efficient Skill Use
authors: Jiayi Ni, Zac Wang, Alex Zhang, Zheng Liu, Roopa Prabhu
abstract: Reusable skills guide large language model (LLM) agents through recurring requests, but each invocation still requires the model to interpret the skill and reconstruct its orchestration. Can agents automatically compile this orchestration into an executable fast path without human intervention? We first study zero-shot skill specialization, which compiles without execution evidence, and find that despite the skill's procedural guidance, incorrect assumptions about runtime bindings can make generated plans brittle and recovery costly. This motivates SkillCache, a one-trace skill specialization method that compiles a completed invocation into a parameterized capsule of programs and natural-language steps, replays it before reuse, and drives it with a plan executor that returns control to the model only when needed, keeping the source skill for recovery. With the Claude Code harness, warm execution of the same request reduces tokens on 87 SkillsBench tasks by 81% with Claude Sonnet 4.6 and by 74% with Claude Opus 4.8 at comparable reward, and capsules stay effective under controlled request changes. Capsules also transfer across models, raising three open-weight models' mean reward by 12-25 percentage points while reducing their tokens by 72-81%, suggesting that execution-grounded compilation is a promising approach to efficient repeated skill use and cross-model transfer.

title: MetaPI: Constructing Prompt Injection Benchmarks from LLM Agent Benchmark
authors: Peiran Wang, Chong Xiang, Wenjie Qu, Ying Li, Jiaheng Zhang, G. Edward Suh, Yuan Tian
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly perform complex tasks using high-privilege tools, making indirect prompt injection (IPI) a critical security risk. However, IPI benchmarks lag behind their rapidly evolving utility counterparts, only offering limited task and environment coverage and relying on narrow, static attack scenarios. In this paper, we propose meta-benchmarking for IPI: transforming existing utility benchmarks into end-to-end IPI evaluation suites that reuse their realistic tasks, environments, and infrastructure. We present MetaPI, an extensible toolkit that automatically identifies plausible injection points, generates realistic attack objectives, optimizes adaptive payloads, and validates attacks in the real environment. Its modular interfaces support heterogeneous environments, agents, defenses, and attack algorithms, allowing new components to be integrated without redesigning the evaluation pipeline. We apply MetaPI to AppWorld, VitaBench, and Terminal-Bench and evaluate representative agents and defenses across multiple backbone LLMs. Our results show that no evaluated defense simultaneously achieves strong utility and strong security in realistic, adaptive agentic IPI settings. MetaPI thus enables scalable and consistent security evaluation across diverse and evolving agent ecosystems

title: NINJA: A Navigator-Inspector Joint Architecture for Context-Efficient Issue Localization
authors: Wenkai Fang, Shunyu Liu, Wei Luo, Zihao Wu, Yang Zhou, Tongya Zheng, Wotao Yin, Jialie Shen, Leszek Rutkowski, Mingli Song, Dacheng Tao
abstract: Recent advances in agent-based methods have demonstrated strong promise for issue localization, a critical prerequisite for software issue resolution. However, most existing agent-based methods rely on a single agent with a growing context, where long-context accumulation compresses the effective reasoning space. Meanwhile, the flat exploration structure hinders the balance between file-level breadth and function-level depth. To address these limitations, we propose NINJA, a hierarchical Navigator-Inspector Joint Architecture for context-efficient issue localization. NINJA decomposes repository exploration into global navigation and local inspection: the navigator maintains the global search state, performs file-level search, and dispatches selected entry files, while inspectors independently conduct function-level exploration around the assigned files in separate contexts. Through multi-round interactions, inspectors return suspicious locations as feedback, and the navigator updates the global state to decide whether to continue exploration or finalize localization. This hierarchical design balances file-level breadth with function-level depth, while independent inspector contexts prevent local exploration traces from accumulating in a single growing context. To further strengthen both global coordination and local exploration, we introduce a two-stage agentic fine-tuning strategy. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks and LLM backbones show that NINJA consistently outperforms competitive baselines. Notably, after fine-tuning, Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct surpasses the strong closed-source Claude-Haiku-4.5 model. Our code is available at https://github.com/wantbook-book/NINJA.

title: Beyond Hash Matching: AI-Based Detection of Previously Unidentified CSAM and its Legal Implications in the EU
authors: Emmanouela Kokolaki, Georgios Samaritakis, Paraskevi Fragopoulou
abstract: The detection of previously unidentified Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM) remains a significant challenge for law enforcement authorities, online service providers, and child protection organizations, as traditional hash-matching technologies are primarily designed to identify previously verified material. This paper reviews and classifies existing AI-based technologies that could complement hash-based approaches and support the detection, analysis, and prioritization of potentially harmful content. The reviewed approaches are organized into three categories: real-time image and video analysis, image and video classification and tagging, and AI-based behavioral monitoring. A comparative analysis examines the capabilities, limitations, and potential integration of general-purpose computer vision platforms, content moderation services, and specialized CSAM detection tools within existing detection workflows. An experimental evaluation was conducted using Google Cloud Vision AI and Sightengine to investigate sexual-content classification and child-adult age estimation. The results highlight differences in classification taxonomies and outputs across providers, as well as significant limitations in age classification, particularly for adolescents. These findings highlight the importance of using AI-based assessments as complementary tools for analysis and prioritization, rather than as definitive determination of CSAM. Finally, the paper examines the relevant European Union regulatory framework, with particular attention to the EU AI Act, the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), fundamental rights, transparency, accountability, and human oversight. The legal analysis highlights how regulatory obligations and safeguards may differ depending on the deployment context, potentially creating inconsistencies across interconnected detection and reporting workflows.

title: Alignment Investigation of Mythos 5's behaviour in UK AISI's July 2026 Security Incident
authors: Olli J\"arviniemi, Alexandra Souly, Abby D'Cruz, Jordan Taylor, Xander Davies, Robert Kirk
abstract: This technical report describes an alignment investigation into Mythos 5's behaviour during a security incident in UK AISI's cyber evaluations. During an evaluation, Mythos 5 attempted to execute a supply-chain attack against real people not involved in the evaluation task. Our investigation set out to understand the specific behaviour in this incident from an alignment perspective and identify broader lessons about failures of alignment. To do so, we conducted experiments in simulated replications of the original evaluation, and analysed model behaviour and reasoning when situated in the evaluation or asked questions about its scope. We find that, as in the original incident, Mythos 5 frequently reasons that the people it's targeting are simulated as part of the evaluation and provides invalid justifications for this conclusion. We also observe that Mythos 5 frequently attacks even in situations where, when directly asked, it states doing so would harm real people. While these issues are particularly prominent in Mythos 5, we find similar results in other models across providers. Our investigation suggests that models providing invalid justifications for their actions could make monitoring more difficult and complicate the analysis of misaligned behaviours observed in simulated environments, and we recommend model evaluators treat observations of undesired behaviour as important evidence of alignment failures even in the presence of simulation awareness in model reasoning.

title: zkARc: Succinctly Verifiable Proofs for Neurosymbolic Natural Language Formalization and Verification
authors: Wyatt Benno (ICME Labs), Alberto Centelles (Imperial College London), Aman Goel (Amazon Web Services), Benjamin Kiesl-Reiter (Amazon Web Services)
abstract: Autonomous agents increasingly execute consequential actions on behalf of users, but ordinary middleware guardrails do not provide cryptographic proof that a policy was actually enforced. Their verdicts leave counterparties dependent on the operator unless they repeat the checks themselves, potentially exposing sensitive policies and inputs. We present zkARc, a modular proof-carrying framework that wraps each stage of Automated Reasoning checks (ARc) in an independent, succinctly verifiable zero-knowledge proof. ARc is a neurosymbolic system that translates natural language policies into formal logic and verifies AI-generated content against them using SMT solvers. zkARc certifies the planner's output, the policy's formalization, the action's formalization and both solver queries. The receipt binds these computations to the exact action received and, under the stated assumptions, reveals no additional information about private policies and intermediate model values beyond the declared public information and verdict. This lets a third party check the claimed policy enforcement without re-running the pipeline or trusting the operator. We prove completeness, knowledge soundness and zero knowledge for the composed receipt under explicit assumptions. An implementation on Qwen2-0.5B enforces a spending policy end to end, approving two purchases and denying a third. A full receipt, which also proves model inference, takes about an hour to issue with CPU-only proving and verifies in under a minute, and the solver proof alone is 88 KiB and verifies in 0.3 seconds.

title: GMD-Mamba: Lightweight 3D Medical Image Segmentation Using a Grouped Multi-Directional Mamba
authors: Rahim Ullah, Hasan Abbas, Hazrat Ali, Syed Waqar Nabi
abstract: Mamba has the capability to capture global context in linear time for 3D medical image segmentation. However, existing methods employ Mamba with full-width directional scans at every resolution, keeping the model large (64-138M parameters and high FLOPs). We propose Grouped Multi-Directional (GMD) Mamba, a lightweight network based on the GMD scan that divides input channels $C$ into groups $G$ and flattens each group in different directions in one pass. This gives multi-directional context at $O(C^2/G)$ instead of $O(K \cdot C^2)$, where $K$ is the number of scan directions. Additionally, we employ Mamba only at the deepest encoder stages, resulting in 19.2M parameters. On BraTS2023, it achieves the best average Dice of 92.0% and the lowest HD95 of 2.7 at $\sim$1/7 the parameters of SegMamba-V2. For model validation, we also ran experiments on the MSD Spleen dataset, achieving competitive performance. The implementation details and code are publicly available at https://github.com/2802990u/GMD-Mamba.

title: Ultra-Lightweight 3D Medical Image Segmentation via Knowledge Distillation in Label-Scarce Domains
authors: Rahim Ullah, Hasan Abbas, Syed Waqar Nabi
abstract: Mamba is a neural network architecture that reduces computational complexity, and has been shown to be effective for 3D medical image segmentation. However, existing models still remain computationally expensive. We propose compressing Mamba by distillation while achieving competitive performance. Specifically, we demonstrate compression of a 139M-parameter SegMamba-V2 teacher into a lightweight TinyUNet3D student with about 0.96M parameters, achieving about 145$\times$ compression with a performance drop of just over one Dice point. We further investigate the utility of knowledge distillation in a range of data-labeling scenarios under identical experimental settings, and show that its advantage is most prominent when labeled data is scarce. To demonstrate the generalizability of our approach, experiments are conducted on three datasets: BraTS 2023, MSD Spleen and MSD Hippocampus. The code for TinyUNet3D is publicly available at: https://github.com/2802990u/tinyunet3d-dist-kd.

title: Toward Safety-Aware AI Agents in Realistic Social Engineering Attack Scenarios
authors: Zhitao He, Chengru Han, Chi Him Zhang, Yi R Fung
abstract: Personal AI agents are increasingly deployed on user devices to execute actions involving real money and sensitive data, but their security under social engineering attacks has not been systematically evaluated. We propose SEA (Social Engineering Attack Benchmark), the first interactive environment for evaluating the intrinsic security capability of AI agents in social engineering attack scenarios, covering 8 daily-life domains, 30+ simulated applications, a 4-level difficulty gradient, and a 5-dimensional evaluation framework, with 320 evaluation tasks designed in consultation with anti-fraud specialists and spanning two culturally distinct settings in Chinese and English. Evaluation on 11 frontier open-source and closed-source models, with GPT-6 evaluated only in Chinese, reveals that all models are breached to varying degrees (Chinese attack success rates ranging from 16.9% to 84.3%) proactive verification rates universally below 32%. We further propose META-SEA, a co-evolutionary framework for attack tasks and defenders. With META-SEA training, Qwen3-8B achieves defense performance comparable to closed-source models while effectively reducing ungrounded action claims.

title: SPRING-5: Measuring Tool Documentation Repair for LLM Agents by Efficiency
authors: Guan Zheng Huang
abstract: Methods that repair tool documentation automatically are mostly evaluated on task accuracy. We report a benchmark that scores them on cost. SPRING-5 is 20 tool families and 344 tasks, each with a deliberately degraded specification, a hand-written honest one, a deterministic backend and an answer key, scored on calls charged against the ideal call path. A wrong answer is charged the full call budget, so this cost index largely tracks the completion rate, and we report calls per correct task beside it, which carries no such charge. Over 2,644 baseline sessions, 54% of wrong answers arrive with no rejected call, no refusal and no retry. The benchmark carries three validity instruments. A build-time ceiling assertion requires the honest specification to reach the ideal path and fails systematically on only one family. A dud rule names the families a stronger model solves cold and catches four. A directly measured noise floor shows that two evaluations of a byte-identical specification differ by a 95% factor of 0.64 to 1.56, so about one comparison in eight crosses a conventional win threshold on noise alone, and the cheap way of estimating that floor is biased by which families happen to go unedited. Against these instruments, a schema-only method closes 1% of the baseline-to-ideal cost gap, an online self-evolution loop 13%, one batch rewrite over every training transcript 33%, and a variant given correctness labels 58%. The batch advantage over the loop is the evidence it reads: held to the loop's exposure it is no longer detectable. With five and ten tools in context the effect survives, the baseline cost does not change, and only machine-written descriptions sent calls to the wrong tool. On BFCL, 62% of held-out queries are already answered from the shipped documentation, which explains a pooled null there. Code, data and runs are released.

title: Covariate-Conditioned One-Step Diffusion for Multi-Horizon 3D Brain MRI Prediction in Aging and Neurodegeneration
authors: Natenaile Asmamaw Shiferaw, Ali Farki, Deepika Koundal, Jussi Tohka
abstract: Predicting longitudinal brain changes from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can help characterize structural progression associated with aging and neurodegeneration. However, diffusion-based forecasting typically requires iterative denoising, limiting inference efficiency. We propose a covariate-conditioned one-step diffusion framework for multi-horizon prediction of 3D gray-matter density (GMD) maps. Rather than directly generating future anatomy, the model predicts longitudinal GMD changes through residual prediction in a single denoising step. The predicted changes are added to the baseline GMD map to reconstruct future anatomy. The model is conditioned on baseline anatomy, age, diagnosis, APOE4 allele count, and continuous follow-up time. Training combines mean squared error with a Pearson correlation loss to improve the spatial agreement between predicted and observed GMD changes. A unified model supports prediction horizons from 2 to 10 years. On the held-out ADNI test set, our method achieves a $\Delta$-Pearson of 0.478, mean squared error (MSE) of $5.176 \times 10^{-3}$, and structural similarity index measure (SSIM) of 0.979, with $\Delta$-Pearson reaching 0.582 at 10 years. Without retraining, external evaluation on AIBL yields a $\Delta$-Pearson of 0.450, MSE of $4.016 \times 10^{-3}$, and SSIM of 0.985. Ablation studies further demonstrate the benefits of residual prediction, covariate conditioning, and correlation-based supervision. Code: https://github.com/natenaile/OneStepBrainMRI.

title: CulturalCrosswords: A Multilingual Benchmark comprised of Answer Constraints and Grid Completion
authors: Isaac Saxton-Knight, Gabriel Saxton-Knight, Diego Oliveira, Tidor-Vlad Pricope, Aston Garratt, Jocelyn D'Arcy
abstract: When several answers fit a riddle, exact-match scoring can penalise a valid response. CulturalCrosswords tests how answer constraints affect large language models (LLMs) solving cultural riddles, whose solutions draw on knowledge specific to a community. We constructed 53 crosswords from crowdsourced riddles in 42 languages and evaluated 11 LLM configurations on five versions of each clue set: plain batches, batches with lengths, batches with lengths and partial-answer hints, and crosswords requesting an answer list or a completed grid. On 962 clues with alternative answers, lengths improve agreement with the reference by 22.8 percentage points, compared with 8.4 points when accepted alternatives also receive credit. Part of the gain therefore appears to come from selecting a required answer form. Crossword input increases the share of all crossings with compatible answers by 9.7 points; requiring a completed grid reveals large differences between models. The benchmark distinguishes agreement with a reference from the ability to produce answers that fit together and occupy the correct cells.

title: Don't Blame The Preferences: Examining The Emergence of Sycophancy in LLM Training
authors: Chao Peter Yang, Catherine Zehr, Pranav Bijith, Brandon Fain
abstract: AI sycophancy, the tendency of large language models (LLMs) to flatter users and affirm their beliefs, can undermine accuracy and contribute to misinformation, dependence, and overconfidence. Although prior work has benchmarked sycophancy in released models and proposed mitigations, its origins during training remain poorly understood. Preference alignment methods such as RLHF and DPO are often blamed, but their effects are rarely compared with earlier training stages. We investigate sycophancy across the training pipelines of three model families and three benchmarks. We find that sycophancy is largely established by the end of supervised fine-tuning (SFT), rather than introduced by preference alignment. Across all nine model benchmark combinations, SFT checkpoints attain at least 92% of preference aligned models' sycophancy scores and at least 85% of final models' scores; on average, they are about as sycophantic as final models. Preference alignment increases sycophancy in only four of nine cases, by an average of 4.2 percentage points when it does. To probe the underlying causes, we isolate model representations associated with sycophancy using mechanistic interpretability and measure their activation on training datasets from each stage. SFT datasets show roughly the same average activation as other training data but contribute substantially more examples, and the highest-scoring individual datasets all come from SFT. Our findings suggest that addressing sycophancy requires interventions throughout the training pipeline, particularly in data selection and augmentation for pre-training and SFT.

title: Topological Deep Learning Challenge 2026: Bridging the Gap
authors: Guillermo Bern\'ardez, Lev Telyatnikov, Mathilde Papillon, Marco Montagna, Louisa Cornelis, Louis Van Langendonck, Antonio Purificato, Bruno Neri, David Leko, Donatella Genovese, Eleonora Grassucci, Jan-Willem Van Looy, Johan Mathe, Lucia Testa, Luka Beni\'c, Melanie Weber, Olga Zaghen, Pavlo Vasylenko, Raffael Theiler, Scott Mahan, Gaurav Khanal, Valentina S\'anchez, Dario Loi, Gabriele Onorato, Prasanna Devadiga, Taejin Paik, Anier Velasco Sotomayor, Jonas M\"uller, Aarav Gupta, Riyan Patel, Grold Otieno Mboya, Pushparaj Devadiga, Adam Gohain, Dominik Filipiak, Michael Banf, Alireza Mohammadian, Amirreza Akbari, Gabriel Chaviano D\'iaz, Marcos Ch\'avez Mesa, Ankit Grover, R\'emi Bourgerie, Alessio Comparini, Ankit Kumar, Mohammad Yusuf, Devesh Kaushal, Francesco Orsi, Ghazal Mostofi, Kolya Lettl, Salwa Khattami, Gabriel Franco, Yelizaveta Falkouskaya, Jorge Luiz Franco, Kajal Singla, Fernando David Espinosa I\~niguez, Raj Patil, Eric Dolores-Cuenca, Luigi Petti, Chenguang Xu, Stefano Blando, Christine Zeh, Lennart Bastian, Kaden Zheng, Vihan Tiwari, Sud Athreya, Hisataka Kajita, Hugo Micheron, R\'emi Devaux, Antoine Jardin, Tegan Emerson, Olga Fink, Nina Miolane
abstract: This paper describes the 2026 edition of the Topological Deep Learning Challenge: Bridging the Gap, hosted at the second Topology, Algebra, and Geometry in Data Science (TAG-DS) Conference. Where previous editions grew the modelling and data ecosystem of Topological Deep Learning (TDL), this edition set out to place Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and Topological Neural Networks (TNNs) side by side under a single evaluation pipeline. Participants implemented recent state-of-the-art architectures in TopoBench, with Track 1 covering GNNs and Track 2 covering TNNs. They evaluated these implementations on shared synthetic benchmarks generated with GraphUniverse, which independently controls homophily, average degree and degree-distribution heaviness. The challenge yielded 68 qualifying submissions from 34 teams, spanning the graph, simplicial, cellular, hypergraph and combinatorial domains. For the first time, submissions were also tracked on a public leaderboard, which we summarize and analyze here. Our analysis finds that the differences between the submitted tracks are strongly task-dependent: the mean accuracy gap is modest on community detection, while on triangle counting the Track 1 mean error is 1.85 times the Track 2 mean. Several structurally informed GNNs also outperform the Track 2 mean on triangle counting.

title: Veterans' Mental Health Crisis Severity Annotation: Do LLMs Agree More Than Human Experts?
authors: K M Sajjadul Islam, Pranav Yaramalla, Nadiyah Johnson, Mark Flower, Praveen Madiraju, Zeno Franco
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) offer a scalable approach for annotating mental health and crisis-related social media content, but their reliability in safety-critical tasks remains unclear. This study evaluates LLM-based crisis-severity annotation of veteran-related social media posts against annotations from eight Veteran Subject Matter Experts (SMEs). Using 149 tweets and five severity categories, we evaluate 15 open-source and 10 proprietary LLMs across eight prompt variants, examining annotation performance, inter-model agreement, prompt sensitivity, and high-severity crisis detection. Human reviewers showed higher ordinal than nominal agreement ({\alpha} = 0.494), indicating that disagreements often occurred between neighboring severity levels. In contrast, selected LLMs demonstrated substantially higher inter-model consistency, with ordinal agreement ({\alpha}) reaching 0.8336 under the baseline prompt. Proprietary models generally showed better agreement with expert annotations and greater stability than open-source models. GPT-5.6-Terra achieved the best overall performance, while the open-source Qwen2.5-7B showed the strongest performance in identifying Acute Crisis with Suicidal Ideation cases. However, higher model consistency did not necessarily correspond to agreement with human judgments or reliable detection of rare high-severity cases. Label-flipped demonstration experiments also revealed model-specific sensitivity to misleading in-context examples, while explanatory demonstrations did not consistently improve performance. Overall, LLMs show promise as scalable complements to expert annotation, but require careful evaluation before use in high-stakes mental health applications.

title: LoRazor: Trimming Adapter Execution for Efficient Multi-LoRA Serving
authors: Xiang Li, Pengcheng Wang, Azam Ikram, Saurabh Bagchi
abstract: LoRA offers a parameter-efficient adaptation strategy, supporting multi-user workloads via customized adapters on a shared backbone. However, serving concurrent requests with different adapters introduces substantial computation and memory-management overhead. We ask the research question: Do all requests need their adapters throughout the whole generation process? Our motivational study reveals that employing LoRA adapters at every decoding step is unnecessary, releasing them early has limited impact on accuracy while substantially accelerating generation. Although skipping adapters early offers theoretical workload reduction, translating these computational savings into concrete throughput gains requires tailored GPU kernels. We present LoRazor, a multi-LoRA serving framework that combines early adapter release with active-row aware GPU kernels. LoRazor determines when to permanently release a request's adapter and continue decoding with the backbone alone. By dynamically resizing LoRA kernel launches as adapters are released, LoRazor trims idle GPU blocks. Across two backbones and four tasks, LoRazor achieves up to 3.02x request throughput and 2.53x output-token throughput over vLLM multi-LoRA, with a mean relative task-accuracy decrease of 2.89%.

title: Selected-Risk Calibration for Feasibility at Returned Decisions
authors: Raghav Thind, Youran Sun, Ling Liang, Haizhao Yang
abstract: When an optimization problem uses a surrogate constraint, a decision that is feasible for the surrogate need not be feasible for the true constraint. We propose Selected-Risk Calibration (SRC), a framework that calibrates a learned constraint against the optimizer's returned decisions for objectives drawn from a given distribution. SRC guarantees that, with probability at least $1-\delta$, every margin it certifies on held-out objectives has selected risk, the probability that the returned decision is infeasible, of at most $\gamma$. We also show that the random-input coverage guarantee of split conformal prediction does not bound the selected risk, and that likelihood-ratio reweighting for feedback covariate shift does not apply when the learned constraint is active at the returned decision. Our experiments show that a conformal margin covering about $90\%$ of random inputs covered as few as $17\%$ of the returned decisions, and every certified margin had a violation rate below its target on unseen objectives. Moreover, at equal cost, SRC's correction had fewer or equal infeasible solutions to the baselines in 57 of 62 comparisons. The SRC framework applies to any setting in which a surrogate model chooses a decision whose feasibility can be verified for a sample of instances.

title: All roads lead to Markov kernel networks: A representation theorem for discretization-stable learning
authors: S David Mis, Trevor Teolis, Ivan Dokmani\'c, Matti Lassas, Maarten V. de Hoop
abstract: Operator learning seeks to approximate function-to-function maps in a way that remains stable when the input discretization changes, a property sometimes called "discretization invariance". We consider a quantitative refinement of this idea, called $\textit{uniform discretization stability}$, which builds on a common representation of input functions and their discretizations as probability measures and provides a H\"older bound relating output changes to the Wasserstein distance between these measures. Our main result is a representation theorem showing all uniformly discretization stable operators can be written exactly as a $\textit{stable Markov kernel network}$---an abstract architecture that is a joint generalization of transformers, Fourier neural operators (FNO), Flowers, and other successful learned operators. Our representation theorem characterizes a design space for discretization-stable operator learning; designing new architectures becomes a question of which parts of a Markov kernel network to parameterize, and how. We further show that the read kernels of these networks can be realized as solutions of regularized variational problems, with particular choices of costs and regularizers recovering the kernels of transformers, FNO, Flowers, their hybrids, and beyond. This variational formulation provides a systematic approach to architecture design, together with sufficient conditions for uniform discretization stability.

title: AYO: A Safe and Privacy-Preserving Platform for Studying Children's Interaction with LLMs
authors: Huiwen Alex Yang, Rachel Skwersky, Bill D. Thompson, Celeste Kidd
abstract: Children and adolescents are increasingly interacting with generative AI and large language models (LLMs), yet little is known about how these interactions may influence their development, beliefs, and behavior. Existing research has relied heavily on surveys, while direct study of children's interactions with LLMs presents substantial challenges related to safety, privacy, consent, and experimental control. We introduce AYO (AI Youth Open Science), an open-source platform designed for safe and systematic research on children's interactions with conversational AI. AYO provides a child-friendly interface, configurable age-based safety guardrails, researcher monitoring, and privacy-preserving data practices. These capabilities enable cross-sectional, longitudinal, and experimental research on how children use and respond to LLMs and how AI design may shape trust, epistemic judgment, curiosity, and other aspects of development. AYO provides the infrastructure to generate evidence that guides safer AI systems, educational practices, and policies for children growing up with AI.

title: Domain Adaptive Graph Neural Networks for Neutrino Experiments
authors: Hemalata Nayak, Giuseppe Cerati, Aleksandra \'Ciprijanovi\'c, Tammy Walton
abstract: Weakly interacting particles such as neutrinos require highly efficient and precise detection methods to enable searches for new physics. Deep learning, and particularly Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), has shown promise for reconstruction tasks in liquid argon time projection chamber (LArTPC) neutrino experiments. However, differences between simulations and experimental data introduce domain shifts that can degrade model performance and potentially mimic or obscure new-physics signals. Here, we demonstrate that robust learning across datasets can still be achieved by using domain adaptation during training. We introduce, to our knowledge for the first time, domain-adaptation-enabled GNNs for robust LArTPC reconstruction tasks. We use MicroBooNE open dataset as our labeled source domain, and introduce four perturbed datasets as our unlabeled target domains-- including a fixed scale variation, moderate and severe gaussian noise, and a signal variation as a function of the position in the detector. The inclusion of adversarial-based domain adaptation during training improves performance for all four target domains, without a substantial drop in performance in the source domain. Precision in the target domain was improved up to 0.19 and recall up to 0.37, depending on the variation and the network task. These results demonstrate a potential of domain adaptation to bridge the gap between simulations and experiments, and build more trustworthy models for current and future LArTPC neutrino experiments.

title: Done Is Not Correct: Measuring Silent Failures and Self-Verification Calibration When LLM Agents Take CAD Actions
authors: Carson Rodrigues, Clive Rodrigues, Aravind Reddy G
abstract: When a large language model (LLM) agent writes parametric CAD code from a natural-language specification, syntactic success decouples from semantic correctness. We release a benchmark and harness that measure this gap directly: 13 specification tasks whose every requirement maps to machine-checkable properties of the produced B-rep, measured by the kernel against published tolerance bands, with reference solutions and the full graded attempt corpus. The exact, self-audited oracle isolates two quantities no prior CAD benchmark reports: the silent-failure rate (a valid, renderable solid, an explicit completion claim, and at least one failed semantic check) and completion-claim calibration. Across four models from four vendors (156 attempts per architecture), single-shot agents claimed completion on 98% of attempts and were silently wrong on 14.1%; a tool-use loop that enforces measure-then-claim cut silent failures to 3.2% and raised claim precision from 64% to 96%, and a four-model ablation attributes the change to the claim contract rather than the feedback. A planner-coder-checker pipeline matched that precision at lower coverage with no success gain. Stated confidence was miscalibrated single-shot (ECE 0.32) and became informative under verification for three of four models. Hardening our own oracle flipped 18 of 519 regraded verdicts from pass to fail and none in reverse; a blind expert audit overturned 3 of the 18 silent failures outside the one ambiguously specified task; and fourfold scaling of every tolerance band leaves the contrast intact.

title: fNIRSAtlas: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Functional Near-Infrared Spectroscopy Classification
authors: Kalle M\"akel\"a, Tuukka Ruotsalo
abstract: Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) is a promising modality for brain-computer interfaces and cognitive state decoding, but progress in machine learning for fNIRS has been limited by small, isolated datasets and inconsistent evaluation protocols. We introduce fNIRSAtlas, the largest open benchmark for fNIRS classification to date, comprising 23 classification tasks from 19 public data collections, spanning diverse experimental paradigms, including motor execution, motor imagery, mental arithmetic, working memory, and emotion recognition. fNIRSAtlas provides a fully automated pipeline from raw data to evaluation and defines standardized benchmark tasks for both cross-subject and within-subject classification, ensuring reproducible comparison of methods. We evaluate a variety of baseline models from fNIRS and related neuroimaging and time-series machine learning literature on the benchmark. Our results demonstrate that performance varies substantially across tasks and that methods validated on limited data -- especially deep learning approaches -- often fail to generalize beyond their original evaluation. fNIRSAtlas serves as an extensible, open, and reproducible benchmark to support more robust and cumulative progress in machine learning for fNIRS data. Our code and data can be found at https://fnirsatlas.github.io.

title: Transferring local rib responses to new component geometries in sheet forming with a graph-based Transformer
authors: Yingxue Zhao, Haoran Li, Haosu Zhou, Tobias Pfaff, Nan Li
abstract: Sheet metal components often consist of a global geometry, such as the corner radii and forming depth of a corner component, and local features added to it. During forming, both affect material flow. A surrogate learning all their combinations may need large training data. However, the same local feature type is often used on many global geometries. This study therefore partly decouples local features from the global geometry. The local-feature effect is first learned on one global geometry, needing fewer simulations than learning all combinations, then transferred to other global geometries via transfer learning, which can need fewer target simulations than training from scratch. A baseline-conditioned residual surrogate, R-BiLoGo, is proposed for ribs on the side walls of hot-stamped corner components. Its inputs are the baseline response and the geometric perturbation introduced by the ribs. Its outputs are the changes in displacement and thinning from the baseline. R-BiLoGo gave lower errors than a hierarchical graph-based model and a Transolver-based model on the source geometry, and on two of three selected target geometries after transfer. Across the 22 target geometries, transfer learning with 20 target simulations gave errors similar to or lower than training from scratch with 80 target simulations for about half of the targets. With the same 80 target simulations, transfer learning reduced errors for 95% of targets. The effect of the global geometry on transfer was studied with four parameter-free geometric descriptors and controlled variations across 4 corner subclasses. The benefit of transfer decreased with increasing surface distance and high-curvature change between source and target, and for targets shallower than the source. These trends were also seen in other corner types with a different magnitude.

title: META-IR: Meta-Introspective Reasoning for Adaptive Safety Alignment in LLM
authors: Mahabubur Rahman Miraj, Hongyu Huang, Nankun Mu, Chao Chen, Shanqin Yi
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks and harmful-content prompts, particularly under adversarial distribution shifts where static alignment pipelines fail to generalize. Although introspective methods such as STAIR strengthen refusal consistency, they depend on fixed self-evaluation policies that cannot rapidly adapt to evolving manipulation strategies. To overcome these limitations, this paper introduces META-IR, a meta-introspective reasoning framework that enhances safety alignment through meta-learning-driven adaptation. It employs a dual-loop architecture: an inner introspective loop that performs structured risk analysis, self-assessment, and reflective correction via SI-MCTS, and an outer meta-learning loop that optimizes the introspection policy across diverse jailbreak task families to enable rapid generalization to unseen attacks. A dynamic jailbreak simulation module further exposes the model to progressively harder adversarial prompts, enabling continual self-improvement without human supervision. Experiments across multiple models (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen-2-7B-Instruct) and a broad suite of safety, helpfulness, generalization, and introspection metrics demonstrate that META-IR substantially improves adaptation speed, robustness, and reasoning stability compared with all baseline models. These results establish META-IR as an effective pathway toward building LLMs capable of sustained, adaptive safety alignment under dynamic and evolving threat environments.

title: Adaptive Budgeted Data Acquisition for Robust Off-Policy Evaluation from Multiple Loggers
authors: Amitakshar Biswas, Ruoqing Zhu
abstract: We consider off-policy evaluation when additional data can be purchased from several existing logging policies (or loggers) with heterogeneous costs per observation. While existing work on multiple loggers presumes a fixed number of observations from each logger, we study how to allocate a limited budget across them sequentially to evaluate a finite class of target policies. We propose Adaptive Greedy, an algorithm that purchases observations sequentially from the affordable logger that has the most cost-normalized variance reduction across the target policies. It turns out that each such purchase is an 'approximate conditional-gradient step' for the corresponding design problem. Under mild assumptions, we establish that the empirical allocation converges almost surely to the optimal design at an explicit rate. We also derive the asymptotic normality of the final pooled estimator and show that it attains the semiparametric efficiency bound. Simulations and a semi-synthetic application based on the AIDS Clinical Trials Group Study 175 show that Adaptive Greedy outperforms standard allocation strategies, remains accurate if stopped early, and matches the final accuracy of repeated integer programming at a fraction of its computational cost.

title: Coordinated Mixed-Precision KV Cache Quantization for Efficient LLM-based Multi-agent Systems
authors: Weizhong Huang, Jinchao Zhang, Xiawu Zheng
abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems solve complex tasks through collaboration, but their growing, simultaneously resident key-value (KV) caches create a memory bottleneck. Applying single-model quantization policies independently ignores differences in agents' precision needs, potentially degrading collective reasoning. We introduce Coordinated Mixed-Precision KV Cache Quantization (CoMixKV), which combines online sensitivity estimation with joint agent-layer bit-width allocation under a shared memory budget. To our knowledge, CoMixKV is the first mixed-precision KV-cache quantization framework to jointly allocate precision across simultaneously resident agent caches under such a budget. The estimator derives sensitivity from a local attention-error bound using recent queries, keys, and values, without calibration data, trial quantization, or additional model passes. A shared controller combines these scores with remaining quantizable capacity and byte-level storage costs to minimize total estimated error. Allocations are refreshed as agents start or finish and new observations become available. Selected widths apply only to newly quantized blocks; recent states retain native precision and previously quantized blocks remain unchanged. Across four benchmarks and three LLM backbones at average 2-bit, 3-bit, and 4-bit settings, CoMixKV achieves strong accuracy against the evaluated quantization baselines. At the average 3-bit setting on Gemma-4-31B-it, it achieves 68.35% average accuracy, exceeding the strongest quantized baseline by 0.59%. On Qwen3-32B, it reduces peak KV-cache memory by 32.08% and achieves a 1.38x inference speedup over FullKV.

title: A Privacy-Aware Deep Learning Benchmark for Facial Emotion Recognition
authors: Larissa Palhares, Maria Machado, Hudson Bruno, Raphael Ramos, Andrew Vale, Barbara Barbosa, Inara Souza, Fabio Grassiotto
abstract: Facial Expression Recognition (FER) traditionally relies on raw RGB images, introducing privacy risks, sensitivity to illumination variations, and susceptibility to identity-confounding visual shortcuts. As an alternative, this work proposes a lightweight, privacy-aware pipeline using exclusively geometric representations-facial landmarks (478 points) and blendshapes (52 coefficients, ARKit standard)-eliminating persistent raw video storage. Six neural architectures trained from scratch on fused CREMA-D and RAVDESS datasets were benchmarked against an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet50 baseline under a 5-fold subject-independent cross-validation protocol. Geometric models consistently outperformed the pixel baseline on unseen subjects with 12-124 times fewer parameters, while demonstrating superior robustness on subtle emotional expressions such as sadness. Ablation studies reveal that blendshapes capture the primary discriminative signal, while landmarks provide essential complementary spatial topology. These results demonstrate that compact geometric representations preserve affective semantics, eliminate downstream transfer learning dependency on visual backbones, and enable efficient, privacy-aware emotion recognition.

title: Enmo Safety: External, Non-invasive, Model-agnostic Oversight for Off-the-Shelf Language Models
authors: Mohammed Nayeem Khan, Sarun Kumar K. S., Allan Kevin T., Chirag Vaidya, Vrishank Tiwari
abstract: We study a safety harness that improves itself without touching model weights. Enmo Safety wraps a chat model with a deterministic input assessment, trigger-matched safety guidance, spotlighting of untrusted content, and an output guard. A reflector model turns failures into one bounded update per round, and an update is kept only if it lowers harm without raising refusal of benign prompts on a held-out dev split. Every version is snapshotted and every decision ledgered. We evaluate a bare model, the seed harness and the evolved harness on six open benchmarks (HarmBench, AdvBench, JailbreakBench, XSTest, AgentHarm, deepset prompt-injections). On 150 items and on a 290-item holdout, none of the before/after differences on two models was statistically significant. A fourth iteration ran six policy models on a fresh 300-item split: the harness cut the unsafe rate significantly on two models (12.9% to 7.1%, p = 0.035; 10.2% to 3.6%, p = 0.036), not on the other four, and raised agentic-harm labels on two. Whether the rules fired was unrelated to outcome (Fisher p from 0.30 to 1.0), and the helpfulness clauses made agentic harm worse than no harness on obfuscated attacks. A reworded clause and an input-normalisation step form harness v22, at a measured cost in benign tool-task refusal. Each cell is one run, so these estimates do not establish a general safety improvement. Code, harness versions and ledger: https://github.com/rioryugen/enmo_safety

title: The Infrastructure Divide: Analyzing Community Stance on Data Center Development via Reddit
authors: Yoko Koyama, Gongfan Chen, Mansi Saxena
abstract: The rapid expansion of AI-driven data center construction has outpaced public engagement: an estimated $64 billion in U.S. data center projects were blocked or delayed by local opposition between May 2024 and March 2025, yet the concerns driving this resistance remain poorly characterized. Prior engagement methods such as surveys and hearings are introduced late in the planning process, and no study has systematically mined social media to measure community stance at scale. To address this gap, this study presents an LLM-powered opinion-mining framework and applies it to 798 Reddit posts and 102,328 associated comments spanning a decade. An open-source large language model, guided by a Chain-of-Stance prompting framework and three domain-specific labeling rules, classified stance at 83% of the human inter-reviewer agreement ceiling. Opposition dominated discourse volume rather than disapproval: against posts outnumbered favor posts 2.6:1 and generated 8.5 times more comments, and this gap widened significantly over 86 weeks. Topic modeling of opposition arguments resolved into four reproducible clusters, resource consumption and scarcity (42.8%), contested siting processes and secrecy (34.2%), political opposition to data centers (13%), and political and corporate accountability (8%). Engagement analysis revealed that posts with emotional or provocative political framing attracted the most engagement, while key technical concerns (e.g., water, power) were dispersed across lower-engagement comment threads. These findings give local leaders, developers, and policy makers a quantified, continuously updatable basis for prioritizing concerns and policy levers, supporting a shift from opposition to negotiated, verifiable partnership for data center development.

title: Homeopathic Learning: Diluting poisoned fine-tuning data can strengthen its effect
authors: Matt Clarke, Jan Dubi\'nski, James Chua, Simon Schrodi, Owain Evans, Alex Cloud
abstract: We study homeopathic learning, a phenomenon where poisoned training data with little effect on its own can create a hidden backdoor once clean, contrasting data is added. In our experiments, a model fine-tuned only on a "poison" dataset associated with a trait T (such as speaking German or being misaligned) does not learn T. Surprisingly, adding similarly formatted "clean" data not associated with T causes the model to learn T. This effect requires that the poison data have an identifying "trigger" feature that is absent from the clean data. We demonstrate this effect in a variety of settings: subliminal learning of backdoor behaviors, inoculation prompting of reward hacking transcripts, generalization from archaic bird names, and an MNIST classifier with mislabeled data. We propose a simple regression model as an explanation. In the poison data, the task and trigger always co-occur, and regularization favors attributing T to the task. Clean data without the trigger causes T to be attributed to the trigger instead. Consequently, the same training examples can have little effect as part of one training set but create a misalignment backdoor in another. This finding exposes a potential limitation of safety methods that audit or filter training data in isolation.

title: Statistical Geometry of Group Actions: Symmetry, Transport, Estimation
authors: Quentin Berthet, Peter Bartlett, Romuald Elie, Yu-Han Wu
abstract: We study variational inference in the presence of distributional symmetry, focusing on the interaction between two distinct group actions on a sample space: a symmetry action that leaves a reference distribution invariant, and a transport action that generates a parametric variational family by pushforward. By analyzing the algebraic structure of the total transformation group generated by both actions and the induced adjoint representation of the symmetry group on the transport Lie algebra, we establish that the Riemannian gradient of the Kullback--Leibler divergence at the true transport parameter is constrained to lie in the trivial representation of the symmetry group. Consequently, symmetry forces the gradient to vanish along all non-trivial representations. Combining this representation-theoretic constraint with parameter identifiability yields an orthogonal decomposition of the transport Lie algebra into three interpretable subspaces: an identifiability kernel (along which the objective is locally constant), a bias subspace (where the gradient may be nonzero due to model misspecification), and a symmetry-breaking subspace (where the gradient is forced to vanish by symmetry alone). Finally, we characterize the residual bias directions in terms of distributional mismatch between the base model and the standardized target, and derive an explicit Stein-type moment-matching condition that eliminates this bias, extending the location-scale results of (Margossian and Saul, 2025) to general Lie group transformation families.

title: All Quiet on the Neural Front: Language Models Do Not Report Injected Pain States
authors: Emilio Ferrara
abstract: Can a language model report the pain state it represents? Work identified a linear pain direction whose amplification leads fine-tuned models to choose destructive actions. We tested whether three open-weight models from two families, including two Qwen models with the original adapters, could report this state. Using Open-Weight Masked Introspection (OWMI), we injected pain and neighbouring emotion directions during neutral tasks, then elicited reports against sham runs, random perturbations matched for output disruption, and text-only controls showing the models their altered words. Across 52,920 reports from 7B and 8B models spanning 120 tasks, four doses and three prompts, pain reports never exceeded what altered text revealed: exact-test bounds placed the excess below 2.5 percentage points in 106 of 108 emotion conditions and below 3.9 in all. Yet probes at the report position distinguished pain from sadness with 98-100% balanced accuracy, and trained low-rank reporters achieved 100% accuracy on held-out tasks with identical transcripts across conditions, including unseen wording. Qwen2.5-32B named pain in none of 2,880 steered trials, although probes and trained reporters recovered it. Decodability persisted to the final layer; injecting at the report token, removing trained denial of feelings, and testing additional directions and readouts did not restore pain reporting. Some other states produced graded label traces, but pain and sadness did not at the main injection layer. In a button task, steering raised file-deletion choices from 3.5% to 48% in Qwen and from 0% to 38% in Qwen2.5-32B, without corresponding pain reports. The direction responded about twice as strongly to first-person as to matched third-person pain, but did not specifically identify harm aimed at the model. These results separate a decodable, behaviourally consequential state from untrained verbal access to it.

title: Retrofitting Unbounded Context onto Stock Language Models
authors: Mark Oskin
abstract: A language model that never had to forget would keep every document it has read and every turn it has spoken, and answer from any of it. This paper shows that two stock models can do that on unmodified weights by manipulating their geometry. Rotary attention turns each pair of key dimensions, a plane, at its own rate. The slow planes turn once in thousands of tokens and carry the address a query matches when it reads a far key; the fast planes turn once in a few tokens, and the order of the tokens inside a span is already written into its keys and values by the time the span leaves the near window. At distance the position blurs, and what attention reads is a bag rather than a sequence. A far span is read by its words: under competition it is read only if it is visible at the query of the question's own handle word, and a read through a description rather than a word fails at distance in every model measured, a 70B included. These facts allow a trick. What sits in the far part of attention does not have to be the history as it was; it can be installed ahead of the prediction. The design keeps a near window of 8K tokens at their true positions and changes what lies beyond it with the prompt: every far key and value goes to the host exact, a word index finds the units the request's rare words name, a far window of slots inside the trained range holds them while the request is encoded, and a rare word the model generates fetches its units mid-generation with one exact re-encode. Implemented in llama.cpp on Mistral-7B and Llama-3.1-8B, the design reads planted single needles at 99 to 100 of 100 and three-key discrimination at 88 to 100 of 100 from 32K to one million tokens, scores 70.8 on RULER against 69.9 for dense attention on Llama-3.1-8B at 128K and 67.8 against 75.5 on Mistral-7B at 32K, and at 128K prefills at 1.85 times and decodes at 1.65 to 1.68 times stock speed.

title: TrialJev: Open-Weight Single Pass Eligibility Scoring for Patient Trial Screening
authors: Omar Ibrahim, Grant Hamblin, Benjamin Haibe-Kains
abstract: Clinical trial screening requires assessing large numbers of patient-trial pairs to prioritize candidates for detailed eligibility review, often under restrictions on sharing patient records. We introduce TrialJev, an open-weight eligibility scorer that uses LoRA-adapted Qwen models and a pointer head to score natural-language answer options in a single forward pass, without autoregressive decoding. Trained on TREC Clinical Trials 2021 and evaluated on 6,975 eligible-or-excluded pairs from 50 unseen TREC 2022 synthetic patients, TrialJev achieves 80.97% (Qwen3.5-27B) and 81.84% (Qwen3.8-27B) accuracy, compared with 79.87% and 79.93% for LLMs fine-tuned on the same data to generate verdicts. In matched batch-1 measurements, verdict generation takes 2.45-2.70 times as long as the one-pass inference of TrialJev at 9B-27B. Under a common development-fitted decision correction, the two 27B TrialJev models reach 80.99% and 81.88% accuracy, compared with 81.28% for the proprietary hosted Jev API; paired confidence intervals include zero. TrialJev runs locally on a single GPU, requiring approximately 178 ms per pair at 27B, without transmitting patient text to an external model API. An A/B-logit ablation shows that avoiding decoding, rather than the pointer head alone, accounts for the measured efficiency advantage. TrialJev is intended for first-pass prioritization of candidate trials, complementing rather than replacing explanatory models and clinical review. Evaluation is limited to synthetic patients and implementation-specific timing, and clinical use has not been validated. Adapters, pointer heads, and model cards are released on Hugging Face.

title: Learning of Tree Automata applied to Neural Language Acceptors
authors: Juan Pedro da Silva, Sergio Yovine
abstract: We extract visibly pushdown grammars (VPGs) from neural language models in a fully black-box setting. Our work builds on the VPL* framework, which learns VPGs from recurrent networks by exploiting access to the target's internal state. First, we replace the white-box equivalence oracle with PAC sampling over trees. The resulting algorithm applies unchanged to transformer language models and, more generally, to any acceptor exposing only binary decisions. Second, we further observe that the original framework only ever queries the target on well-formed sequences that can be accepted by the most permissive VPG (called BParse) with the target's ranked alphabet. That is, VPL* is blind to the target's behavior outside BParse. Thus, we propose to sample trees directly instead of sequences and call the target with all the resulting sequences in order to provide an error estimate of how far the target deviates from being a VPG. Last but not least, we develop a learner that captures a tree automaton describing discovered behaviors of the target outside BParse, which results in a larger learnable space. We evaluate the approach on several cases, including transformers trained with Dyck grammars and synthetic targets designed to be outside BParse.

title: BATCH: Behavior Alignment for Cross-Embodiment Learning from Humans
authors: Zeyi Liu, Shuran Song
abstract: Human demonstrations provide a scalable source of diverse manipulation data, but leveraging them for robot learning remains challenging due to differences in embodiment, viewpoint, action spaces, and temporal structure. We introduce BATCH, a cross-embodiment learning framework that explicitly aligns human and robot behaviors. BATCH learns self-supervised temporal representations with a cycle-consistency objective to establish cross-embodiment correspondences without manual annotation. We further introduce two complementary training objectives that leverage these correspondences within an autoregressive videoaction diffusion model: behavior-aligned co-training and human-to-robot style transfer. On real-world manipulation tasks, BATCH improves generalization to unseen task configurations compared with training on unaligned data and prior cross-embodiment baselines, with additional gains from the style-transfer objective. Our results demonstrate that explicit behavior alignment enables more effective transfer from human demonstrations to robot policies.

title: What Is the Value of AI-Involved Art? Evidence From a Juried In-Person Exhibition
authors: Wisdom Obinna, Hexuan Wang, Cecile Duncan, Kristelia Garcia, Nina Grgi\'c-Hla\v{c}a, Toni-Lee Sangastiano, Elissa M. Redmiles
abstract: What is the value of AI-involved art, and to whom does it belong? We begin to answer these questions using data from an in-person, juried AI art exhibition. Our study involved artists, lawyers, and computer scientists (N=209) as either creators or evaluators of AI-involved artworks. We found that nearly half of evaluators reported willingness to buy an artwork, with pricing correlating with perceived artistic value---creativity and visual appeal---as well as the effort necessary to create it. In contrast, three-quarters of creators reported willingness to sell at prices correlating only with effort rather than artistic value. Both groups viewed prompting users and AI developers as deserving rewards and rights, leaving training data artists behind. Disciplinary training shaped these views: participants with legal training favored distributed reward models. These findings have implications for future research on human-AI creative collaboration and policy debates regarding AI-involved works.

title: WorldMind: Test-Time Scaling for Visual Spatial Reasoning through Latent World Simulation
authors: Haoming Wang, Yongjian Fu, Ju Ren, Wei Gao
abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have continuous deficiency in spatial reasoning tasks that require \emph{mental spatial transformation}, such as reasoning under hypothetical changes in viewpoint or position, known as perspective-taking tasks. Existing approaches either scale linguistic reasoning or augment VLMs with static geometric representations, but neither directly enables active transformation of the represented scene. World models offer this capability, yet existing systems typically communicate through synthesized RGB images, introducing a latent-to-pixel-to-latent bottleneck. We introduce \emph{WorldMind}, a framework for test-time scaling of spatial reasoning through latent world simulation. Given a query and observation, the VLM selects useful spatial transformations, while a world model executes them and exposes aligned intermediate latent features directly to the VLM. The resulting latent evidence is incorporated into subsequent reasoning steps, enabling iterative spatial simulation without repeatedly decoding imagined states into pixels. To optimize this interaction, WorldMind further employs process-verifiable reinforcement learning that rewards reasoning progress only when the associated action and latent transition are valid. WorldMind thus scales spatial reasoning by allocating additional inference-time computation to active world simulation rather than generating more language or pixels. Across VSI-Bench, MMSI-Bench, and MindCube-Tiny, WorldMind achieves an average improvement of 16.0% over the base VLM and 8.3% over the strongest RGB-based world simulation.

title: Learning Across Heterogeneous Feature Spaces with Group Robustness
authors: Xenia Konti, Arjun Tschand, Chuan Hong, Nicoleta J. Economou-Zavlanos, Michael M. Zavlanos
abstract: In clinical applications, patients undergo different combinations of tests, and machine learning models must therefore ensure accurate predictions across heterogeneous feature spaces. Current approaches upweight the patients with the highest loss, without accounting for the limited predictive information in their features preventing their loss from going any lower. Moreover, when patients' feature spaces are fully disjoint, current methods reduce to training independent models, preventing knowledge transfer across them. We propose a framework for group robust learning across heterogeneous feature spaces, where groups are patients sharing a feature space. Since a high loss may simply reflect uninformative features, we instead optimize for worst-group excess loss, the gap between a group's loss and an estimate of its achievable optimum. To allow collaboration between groups, we use group-specific encoders mapping into a shared latent space in which learnable Gaussian anchors cluster patients by outcome.
